chunks: So do not compete for the honor and pride of the world,
and do not be amazed by its adornment and bliss, nor grieve over its hardships and misery,
for its honor and pride will come to an end, its adornment and bliss will perish, and its hardships and misery will cease.
and every period within it has an end, and every living being in it is destined to die.
Is there not a warning for you in the traces of the predecessors, and an insight and lesson in your forefathers, if you use your intellect?
Do you not see that those who passed away from you do not return, and the remaining successors do not remain forever?
ai.seo_question: What is the transient nature of worldly life according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this passage from *Nahj al-Balagha*, Imam Ali (AS) employs the rhetorical device of *muqabala* (parallelism) to contrast the fleeting nature of worldly glory with the permanence of the Hereafter, urging believers to adopt a stance of balanced detachment rather than ascetic withdrawal. He invokes the historical precedent of past generations (*athar al-awwalin*) as a divine lesson (*mudhakkara*), reinforcing the Shia emphasis on using history as a source of spiritual insight (*tadabbur*). This teaching aligns with the concept of *zuhd* (asceticism) not as poverty, but as freedom from the heart's attachment to transient pleasures.

en.sayed-ali-raza: So do not hanker after worldly honour and its pride,
and do not feel happy over its beauties and bounties nor wail over its damages and misfortunate
because its honour and pride would end while its beauty and bounty would perish, and its damages and misfortunates would pass away.
Every period in it has an end and every living being in it is to die.
Is not there for you a warning in the relics of the predecessors and an eye opener and lesson in your fore-fathers, provided you understand?
Do you not see that your predecessors do not come back and the surviving followers do not remain?
